newsitem.title: UK: Grobbelaar becomes focus in soccer bribes case.
newsitem.headline: Grobbelaar becomes focus in soccer bribes case.

text.p: The spotlight falls on former Liverpool goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar again on Wednesday, a day after a court heard he had accepted a bribe for rigging a match to benefit a Far Eastern betting group.

Prosecutor David Calvert Smith is due to continue outlining the case against Grobbelaar, who together with three other defendants stands accused of accepting or giving money to rig matches in the first case of its kind for more than 30 years.

On Tuesday, Calvert Smith said chief prosecution witness Chris Vincent would tell the court how Grobbelaar decided to offer to rig matches after he became embittered by what he considered to be the low wages Liverpool were paying him.

According to Vincent -- a former business associate of Grobbelaar -- the goalkeeper flew to London to pick up 40,000 pounds ($67,000) in cash after Liverpool lost 3-0 at rivals Newcastle in late November 1993.

The money was handed over by fellow defendant and former striker John Fashanu, who along with Malaysian businessman Heng Suan Lim is also accused of making large cash payments to fellow goalkeeper Hans Segers to influence matches.
"Grobbelaar admitted on tape and video that he was indeed party to such an agreement," the prosecutor told the court at the start of a trial which is expected to last eight weeks.

Calvert Smith said large amounts of money had regularly been paid to Fashanu, his wife and Lim from Indonesian accounts controlled by a man known as Johannes Josef, whom he suggested was in control of the syndicate.
"(We) found no evidence to back up any kind of business between Fashanu and the Far East," he said.
Calvert Smith said the jury should not scorn Vincent just because he had decided to turn against Grobbelaar only after they argued about business dealings.

"What Vincent will say on all crucial matters is directly and indirectly supported by independent evidence. We suggest that although he is a witness you may have little sympathy for, what he says is borne out," he said.
The case broke in November 1994 when the Sun newspaper, armed with accusations from Vincent, accused the goalkeeper of being corrupt.

The prosecution is basing its case on 10,000 documents gathered over two years, many of them telephone logs which showed that Fashanu and Lim were in constant contact with both goalkeepers despite protests to the contrary.
The prosecutor said that although there was no guarantee a keeper could throw a match by himself, he was one of the players most likely to be able to influence the result.
"Goalkeepers do make a mistake sometimes, so it may be that the odd deliberate mistake may escape attention," he said.
